sections.bio:
I'm 18 year old technology enthusiast and creative strategist working at the intersection of AI, electronics, and digital innovation.

An engineering student at Delhi Technological University pursuing a B.Tech in Electronics and Communication Engineering, driven by a passion for transforming technical complexity into impactful solutions and engaging narratives. 

My technical interests lie in machine learning, AI systems, and embedded electronics. Learning from first principles gives me a deep sense of purpose.

What drives me:
Building at the crossroads of technology and business strategy
Creating content that shows the real story
Exploring how AI and IoT can solve real-world challenges

I thrive in competitive environments—from quiz competitions to business simulations and hackathons. 

Beyond technology, I’ve developed launch strategies for brands that blend data-driven insights with creative storytelling. My work spans content calendars, media strategy, and audience engagement.I’m always eager to connect with fellow innovators, entrepreneurs, and anyone passionate about leveraging technology for meaningful impact. Whether it’s discussing the latest in AI, exploring startup ideas, or collaborating on creative projects—let’s build something remarkable together.

The classmate or colleague who's best at everything is 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂. They run better models.

The person 2 years ahead of you already uses all 5.

1. 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 (𝙀𝙡𝙤𝙣 𝙈𝙪𝙨𝙠)

Break the problem down to what is actually true, then rebuild.
Musk refused to accept that a rocket costs $65M. He priced the raw materials and found they were about 2% of that. SpaceX exists because of one question.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘁: Instead of "I can't switch careers, I have no experience," ask "what does this role actually require?" It is usually 3 skills, not a degree.

2. 𝗜𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝘾𝙝𝙖𝙧𝙡𝙞𝙚 𝙈𝙪𝙣𝙜𝙚𝙧)
Stop asking how to succeed. Ask how you would guarantee failure, then avoid exactly that.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘁: List what kills careers. Missed deadlines. Zero visibility. No new skills. One toxic relationship. Avoid those 4, and you are already ahead of most people.

3. 𝗖𝗶𝗿𝗰𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 (𝙒𝙖𝙧𝙧𝙚𝙣 𝘽𝙪𝙛𝙛𝙚𝙩𝙩)
Know where your knowledge actually ends. Winning is staying inside that circle, not pretending it is bigger.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘁: Buffett sat out the entire dot com boom. He looked wrong for 2 years and was right for 20. Say no to the "opportunity" you cannot explain in 2 lines.

4. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗙𝗲𝘆𝗻𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗾𝘂𝗲 (𝙍𝙞𝙘𝙝𝙖𝙧𝙙 𝙁𝙚𝙮𝙣𝙢𝙖𝙣)
If you cannot explain it simply to a 12 year old, you do not understand it yet.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘁:  Before your next presentation, explain the idea to someone outside your field. Every place you stumble is a hole in your own thinking, not theirs.

5. 𝗥𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘁 𝗠𝗶𝗻𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝙅𝙚𝙛𝙛 𝘽𝙚𝙯𝙤𝙨)
Fast forward to age 80. Ask which choice you would regret not making.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝘁: Bezos left a comfortable Wall Street job using this one question. Use it for the message you are scared to send and the role you are scared to apply for. Nobody regrets the attempt.

Most people collect information.
Very few collect thinking tools.
Only one of those two compounds.

At Jantar Mantar right now, alongside the tents and slogans, sits a permanent surveillance tower plus mobile camera vans parked in plain sight, filming protesters through rain, meals, even medical breaks. 

A petition before the Delhi High Court alleges police threatened to send that footage to protesters' parents and colleges. Most of those protesters are students.
Here's the irony: the face detection and video analytics tech running those cameras is the same project thousands of engineering students across Delhi are trying to deliver. We're building the exact tools now being pointed at people our own age.

To be fair, that same camera network reportedly helped police identify who was responsible for actual violence at the protest, leading to multiple FIRs. Nobody wants unaccountable vandalism either.

The real gap isn't left vs right. It's that India still has no dedicated law for facial recognition. You can back the police and still want a rulebook before a van like that gets parked at every protest in the country.

#FacialRecognition #AI #TechEthics #Privacy #artificialintelligence #India #Protest

Your best AI teammate is about to get expensive after 19th July. 

So stop using it like a chatbot.  
Use it like a senior operator who’s about to leave and has to document everything.

That’s how I’d use Anthropic Fable 5 right now.

Not for random prompts.  
For leverage.

Here’s the play:

1. Pick one painful business outcome.  
Not “be more productive.”  
Try: “Save 5 hours a week on content, ops, or research.”

2. Give it the full context.  
Calendar. Docs. Files. Notes. Past work.  
The better the inputs, the better the system.

3. Turn one repeat task into a machine.  
Competitor research. Weekly reporting. Content planning.  
Whatever eats time every week, systemize it.

4. Force it to write the SOP.  
Prompts. Workflow. Checklists. Edge cases.  
Build it once, then hand it to cheaper models later.

5. Stress test the output.  
Ask: “What breaks? What’s missing? How do I make this sharper?”  
Then refine until it’s actually usable.

This is the real move.  
Not relying on expensive AI forever.  
Using it to build systems you can scale cheaply.

The founders who win won’t be the ones using AI casually.

They’ll be the ones turning it into operating leverage.

#AI #Startups #Automation #Productivity #FounderMode #India #Claude #Anthropic #Fable

Is AI making you dumb, or is your friend just getting smarter than you, and how to maintain your originality? (Solutions & tools below)

That's the thing nobody's saying out loud.
Because both things are true at the same time.

Yes, AI can hollow out your thinking. Every time you ask it for an opinion before forming one yourself, that muscle gets weaker. Psychologists call it cognitive offloading. 

Your brain stops storing what it knows it can retrieve. Used that way, AI isn't a tool, it's a slow leak.

But then there's your friend. Same college. Same office. Same 24 hours. Somehow producing more, moving faster, thinking sharper. You've noticed. You just haven't said it out loud.
They're not smarter. They figured out the other side of this:

The people quietly getting ahead aren't replacing their thinking with AI they're sharpening it. There's a sequence that changes everything:

Form the opinion first. Then use AI to stress-test it. Draft the rough idea first. Then use AI to sharpen it. Ask the question first. Then use AI to go ten levels deeper.

Keep it and you become a sharper thinker who also moves at machine speed.
The goal was never less AI. It's staying visible in your own output. Leverage the tool. Keep the voice.

If you're a student, in a job, or just watching your smartest friend quietly level up — these are the five tools worth actually understanding, not just installing:
Wispr Flow — wisprflow.ai
Granola — granola.ai 
Reclaim.ai from Dropbox — reclaim.ai 
Raycast AI — raycast.com
Google's NotebookLM — notebooklm.google.com
Redrob AI - redrob.io 
None of these think for you. All of them think with you, if you use them right.

One honest question before you scroll —
Are you using AI to think less, or to think better?
Drop it below. And if this made you think of someone specific, tag them. Might be the most useful thing they see today.

I never thought I’d live to see the day you could buy a piece of Mars.

But here we are.

SpaceX just went public. $135 a share. Closes Day 1 at $161 (+19%). $2 trillion valuation. Largest IPO in human history.

And honestly? i don’t even think about the money when i look at this.

I think about the kid watching a rocket land itself for the first time in 2015 thinking “that’s not real.”

I think about how Starlink is literally giving internet to people who had none.

I think about the fact that this company absorbed an AI division(xAI), owns the world’s biggest satellite network, and is dead serious about putting humans on Mars, and it’s only been 24 years since it was founded in a garage. 
People are calling $SPCX overvalued, Maybe.

But nobody said Amazon  was worth it in 1997 either.
This isn’t a stock pick. This is a front row seat to the most ambitious chapter in human history and for the first time, anyone can buy a ticket.

I’m not your financial advisor. But i am someone who believes the people betting against human ambition have always been wrong.

What side of history do you want to be on?
